Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Stack of `NestedInteger` items; the TOP is the next item in order
Iterating a tree-like structure without recursion
Push in reverse so that the first element ends up on top (a stack pops from the end)
Preserving left-to-right order with a stack
Given API: is this element a number, its value, or its inner list
Unpack lists at the top until an integer is on top (or the stack is empty); `while` because a list can start with another list or be empty
Replace a list on top with its elements, reversed
Guarantees an integer is on top before popping
`hasNext` does the real work, `next` relies on it

p: `[[1,1],2,[1,1]]`. The stack is shown bottom → top; `list[...]` is a nested list not yet expanded. Only the first rows are shown.

blocks.h: Why do the work in `hasNext` rather than `__init__`?
p: Expanding everything in the constructor flattens the whole structure up front: O(total elements) time and memory before the first call, and it ruins laziness if the caller only needs a few values. The lazy stack expands only what is needed and uses memory proportional to the nesting depth plus the current level.

bullets: Empty inner lists such as `[[], 1]`: expanding `[]` pushes nothing, so the loop continues to the `1`.
Deep nesting such as `[[[1]]]`: the loop expands one level per iteration until an integer surfaces.
Time: O(1) amortised per call; each element is pushed and popped once.
Space: O(N) worst case for one huge list; O(depth) when lists are small.

341.takeaway: Nested-list iterator: a stack holding the remaining items in reverse; `hasNext` unwraps lists on top until an integer appears.

p: Frequencies are integers between 1 and n, so they can index an array directly, which removes the log factor. A heap is the answer when the interviewer asks for streaming or when k is tiny.

blocks.h: Why remove the tail before the collision check?
p: With a snake of length 4 chasing its own tail in a 2×2 loop, the head may legally step onto the cell the tail is vacating in the same move. Removing the tail first and then testing `(r, c) in cells` allows this. When the snake ate this turn, the tail stays, so stepping onto it is a collision.

Correct?

Less than 10 seconds since the last print: suppress
Rate limiting by a fixed window
Suppressed attempts do not extend the window
The rule is relative to the last PRINTED time

p: `foo@1, bar@2, foo@3, bar@8, foo@10, foo@11`:

blocks.h: Why only update on a successful print?
p: `foo@10` is rejected because 10 - 1 = 9 < 10. If rejected calls updated the dictionary, `foo@11` would compare against 10 and be rejected, but the correct answer is True because the last print was at 1. Updating on suppressed calls would turn the limit into 'quiet for 10 seconds', a different rule.
The dict grows with the number of distinct messages and never shrinks. If memory matters, keep a deque of (timestamp, message) and a set, evicting entries older than 10 seconds on each call.

359.takeaway: Rate limiter with a hash map of last-printed timestamps; only a printed message updates its entry.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Hits in arrival order; timestamps are non-decreasing, so the oldest is always at the left
Oldest hit is 300 or more seconds old: outside the window `(t-300, t]`
Evict an expired hit in O(1)

p: `hit(1), hit(2), hit(3), getHits(4), hit(300), getHits(300), getHits(301)`:

The window is the last 300 seconds: `(t-300, t]`. At `t = 301` the hit at time 1 is exactly 300 seconds old and must no longer count, which is why the comparison is `<=`; with `<` it would still be counted (answer 4 instead of 3).
For a very high hit rate, store (timestamp, count) pairs or a fixed array of 300 buckets indexed by `timestamp % 300` with their timestamps: O(1) memory instead of O(hits in the window).

bullets: Time: `hit` O(1); `getHits` O(1) amortised (each hit is removed once).
Space: O(hits in the last 300 seconds).

362.takeaway: Hit counter: a deque of timestamps; evict from the left everything older than the window when asked.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: You can never hold more than the two jugs' total capacity
Number theory: the amounts you can pour are combinations `a·x + b·y`
Bézout's identity: `a·x + b·y` can produce exactly the multiples of `gcd(x, y)`

p: Each case checks both conditions:

blocks.h: Why does the gcd decide it?
p: Every fill, empty or pour changes the total water by a multiple of x or y, so the total is always `a·x + b·y` for integers a, b (negative allowed for emptying). By Bézout the set of such values is exactly the multiples of `gcd(x, y)`. The other direction, that every such target ≤ x + y is actually reachable, holds by a constructive pouring strategy.

`x = 0` or `y = 0`: `gcd(x, 0) = x`, so the test reduces to 'target is a multiple of the other jug', capped by capacity. `target = 0` is always reachable (`0 % g == 0`). (If both are 0, `gcd` is 0 and the modulo would fail, but constraints say x, y ≥ 1.)

bullets: Time: O(log min(x, y)) for the gcd.

365.takeaway: Water jug = number theory: the target is reachable iff target ≤ x + y and target is a multiple of gcd(x, y).

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: After sorting, if `a` divides `b` then `a ≤ b`, so only earlier elements can be divisors
Turns divisibility into an ordered relation
Size of the largest divisible subset that ENDS at `nums[i]` (as its largest element)
Index of the previous element in that best chain (-1 if none)
Reconstructing the actual subset, not just its size
Index where the longest chain ends
Follow `prev` back to the start, then reverse

blocks.p: Following `prev` from the best index gives [16, 8, 4] (largest first), and reversing gives `[4, 8, 16]`. A subset of size 3 such as `[4, 8, 16]` is the longest possible here.

blocks.h: Why checking only the previous chain element is enough
p: Divisibility is transitive: if `a | b` and `b | c` then `a | c`. So when `nums[i]` is divisible by the last element of a valid chain, it is divisible by every element before it. That is why `dp[i]` only needs `dp[j]` and `nums[j] | nums[i]`.

bullets: Time: O(n²) for the DP after an O(n log n) sort.

368.takeaway: Largest divisible subset: sort, then LIS-style DP using transitivity of divisibility, with a prev array to rebuild the set.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Sum of the bits WITHOUT carries
XOR is addition modulo 2 per bit
The carries: positions where both bits are 1, moved one place left
Adding the carry may create new carries
Keep only 32 bits; Python integers are unbounded and negatives would otherwise carry forever
If bit 31 is set the 32-bit value is negative: convert to Python's negative number

p: `5 + 7`: each iteration replaces `(a, b)` with `(a ^ b, carries)` until the carry is 0.

`1 + 2`: a = `01`, b = `10`. XOR gives `11`, carry `(01 & 10) << 1 = 0`. Done: 3. Negative case `-1 + 1`: the masked 32-bit pattern of -1 is all ones; the carries ripple through all 32 bits, `a` ends as 0, and the answer is 0. `-2 + -3` returns -5.

In Python `-1` is an infinite string of 1s, so `(a & b) << 1` for negatives never reaches 0 and the loop would not terminate. Masking to 32 bits drops the overflow bit like real hardware, and the final conversion restores the sign.

371.takeaway: Addition without `+`: XOR gives the sum without carries, AND-shift gives the carries; repeat until no carry, masking to 32 bits in Python.

Despite the name this problem counts permutations. With negative numbers allowed the count could be infinite; the follow-up asks what restriction is needed (a limit on sequence length).

head: Code

rows: O(1) random access by index, so `random.choice` is O(1)
Overwrite the removed slot with the last element and update its index
Delete from the middle of an array in O(1) by giving up order
Removes the last element in O(1)
Only the END of a list is cheap to remove
Needs a list/array, not a set

p: Insert 10, 20, 30, then remove 10 and 30. `vals` and `pos` after each operation:

blocks.h: Why swap with the last instead of deleting in place?
p: `list.remove` or `del vals[i]` shifts everything after `i`: O(n). Copying the last element into slot `i` and popping the end is O(1). The price is that order is not preserved, which a set doesn't promise anyway.

If `v` is itself the last element, `last == v`: the code writes `vals[i] = v`, sets `pos[v] = i`, pops it, then deletes `pos[v]`. The order matters: the `pos[last] = i` write happens BEFORE `del self.pos[v]`, so the final delete removes the right entry and nothing stale is left.

380.takeaway: O(1) insert/delete/random: array for random access plus a value→index dict, deleting by swapping with the last element.

p: Matching the earliest possible occurrence of each character leaves the longest remaining part of `t` for the later characters, so it never hurts. If any valid matching exists, the greedy one does too.

For billions of `s` queries against the same `t`, precompute for each character the sorted list of its positions in `t`, then match each `s` by binary searching the next position after the previous one.

Happens with probability exactly 1/cnt: replace the current choice with this index

p: `nums = [1,2,3,3,3]`, `target = 3` has matches at indices 2, 3, 4. The m-th match replaces the choice with probability 1/m and then survives each later match j with probability (j-1)/j:

blocks.h: Why is each index equally likely?
p: Match number m is picked with probability 1/m, and survives match j (j > m) with probability (j-1)/j. The product telescopes: 1/m × m/(m+1) × … × (n-1)/n = 1/n. So every one of the n matches ends with probability exactly 1/n, without knowing n in advance.

Pick time
Extra space

p: If `pick` is called many times and memory is available, the dict of index lists is faster per call. The reservoir version is the answer when the follow-up says 'the array is too large to store extra data'.

398.takeaway: Random pick index = reservoir sampling of size 1: replace the choice with the m-th match with probability 1/m.

Passing context from parent to child
Count the leaf only if it is a left child
The flag is what distinguishes a left leaf

p: You can instead test in the parent whether `node.left` is a leaf. The flag approach keeps the leaf test in one place and handles the root naturally. The common bug is counting any leaf that is the left child of ANY ancestor; only direct left children count.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The current boundary of the explored region, lowest wall first
Dijkstra-like expansion from the weakest point
Water can only escape across the border, so the border is the first wall
Takes the lowest wall: the water level just inside it cannot be higher than this wall
The weakest wall decides the level
Water held on the neighbour = how far the wall exceeds its ground
The neighbour becomes a wall of effective height max(wall, ground)
Water fills low cells up to the wall, so they act as that taller wall

p: 3×6 map. Only pops that discover new cells are shown (each shows the wall height and what water it adds to the neighbours it reveals):

blocks.h: Why a heap and not the two-pointer trick from the 1D problem?
p: In 1D the water level at a cell is min(max-left, max-right). In 2D water can escape in any direction, so the level at a cell is limited by the LOWEST path of walls to the outside. Always expanding from the lowest wall guarantees that when we reach a cell, the wall we came through is the lowest possible barrier, i.e. the true water level.
With fewer than three rows or columns every cell is on the border, and border cells can't hold water.

bullets: Time: O(m·n·log(m·n)), each cell is pushed and popped once.

407.takeaway: 2D rain water: start from the border in a min-heap and flood inward; each new cell holds water up to the lowest wall that reached it.

p: If a limit L allows splitting into at most k parts, any larger limit also does (parts can only get fewer). So feasibility is False…False True…True in `limit`, and binary search finds the smallest True. This pattern, 'minimise the maximum', appears in Capacity to Ship Packages and Koko Eating Bananas.

p: Packing as many elements as possible into each part uses the fewest parts for a given limit. If even the greedy count exceeds k, no arrangement works.

410.takeaway: Minimise the largest subarray sum: binary search on the limit with a greedy 'how many parts' feasibility check.

blocks.h: Why does `cur` grow by exactly one each time?
p: If a run of equal differences has length L, the slices ending at its newest element are the ones starting at each of the earlier positions that leave at least three elements: L - 2 of them. Appending one more element adds one new start, so `cur` increases by one. The sum 1 + 2 + … + m counts all slices in a run, e.g. a run of 5 equal-spaced elements has 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 slices.
`[1,2,3,4,6,8,9,10]` has three runs of equal differences (`1,2,3,4`, then `4,6,8`, then `8,9,10`). `cur` resets at every break, and the total is 3 + 1 + 1 = 5:

413.takeaway: Arithmetic slices: `cur` counts slices ending at i (grows by 1 while the difference holds, resets otherwise) and `total` sums it.
